interactions.label: Why are fatty acids unable to serve as substrates for gluconeogenesis in humans?

params.question: Why are fatty acids unable to serve as substrates for gluconeogenesis in humans?

answers.text: The liver lacks enzymes for β-oxidation during fasting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The liver actively runs β-oxidation during fasting — that is its main source of acetyl-CoA for ketogenesis. The real barrier is downstream of β-oxidation.

answers.text: Fatty acid carbons enter the TCA cycle as acetyl-CoA, and the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is irreversible

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Exactly. Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA cannot regenerate pyruvate or oxaloacetate net. Fatty acid carbons are fully oxidised to CO₂ in the TCA cycle and cannot be used to synthesise glucose.

answers.text: Fatty acids cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fatty acids do cross the inner membrane via the carnitine shuttle. The barrier to gluconeogenesis is not transport but the irreversible loss of carbons as CO₂ once they enter as acetyl-CoA.

answers.text: Gluconeogenesis only accepts three-carbon precursors

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gluconeogenesis accepts substrates of various carbon lengths — oxaloacetate (4C) and amino acids enter at different points. The issue is that acetyl-CoA's two carbons are lost as CO₂ in the TCA cycle, yielding no net glucose.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is that pyruvate → acetyl-CoA is irreversible. Fatty acid β-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA, whose two carbons are lost as CO₂ in the TCA cycle. No net conversion to glucose is possible from this point.
Correct. The irreversibility of the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is a key metabolic commitment — once carbons enter as acetyl-CoA, they are destined for complete oxidation, not gluconeogenesis.

params.question: A patient with uncontrolled type 1 diabetes presents with deep rapid breathing and fruity-smelling breath. Which metabolic derangement best explains these findings?

answers.text: Excessive hepatic glycogenolysis causing severe hyperglycaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Glycogenolysis contributes to hyperglycaemia, but it does not explain the acidosis or the fruity breath. Those signs come from ketone body accumulation, not glucose alone.

answers.text: Unchecked lipolysis and ketogenesis due to absent insulin signalling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Without insulin, glucagon drives maximal lipolysis. The flood of fatty acids overwhelms hepatic β-oxidation, producing acetyl-CoA faster than the TCA cycle can handle. Excess acetyl-CoA is diverted to ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone). Blood pH drops below 7.1 — Kussmaul breathing compensates; acetone gives the fruity odour.

answers.text: Accelerated skeletal muscle proteolysis causing lactic acidosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Muscle proteolysis does occur in fasting but produces amino acids for gluconeogenesis, not the ketoacids responsible for fruity breath. Lactic acidosis has a different clinical picture.

answers.text: Refeeding-induced hypophosphataemia triggering metabolic acidosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Refeeding syndrome occurs when a malnourished patient is fed, causing an insulin surge that drives phosphate and potassium into cells. It is the opposite metabolic scenario — this patient has no insulin at all.

overallFeedback.feedback: In type 1 diabetes without insulin, the metabolic state mimics starvation. Glucagon drives maximal lipolysis → excess acetyl-CoA → ketone body overproduction → metabolic acidosis. Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation; fruity breath is acetone.

Correct. In DKA, absent insulin mimics starvation signals despite abundant blood glucose. The liver generates ketone bodies at a rate that overwhelms buffering capacity. Treatment is insulin, fluids, and potassium replacement.

interactions.label: Which property of the inner mitochondrial membrane is most critical for generati

params.question: Which property of the inner mitochondrial membrane is most critical for generating the proton-motive force used in ATP synthesis?

answers.text: High permeability to small molecules via porins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Porins are a feature of the outer mitochondrial membrane, not the inner. The outer membrane is freely permeable; the inner membrane must restrict proton movement.

answers.text: Impermeability to protons

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The inner membrane's impermeability to protons is what allows the electron transport chain to build up an electrochemical gradient. If protons could leak back freely, no gradient would form and ATP synthase would have no driving force.

answers.text: Presence of glucose-6-phosphatase on its surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Glucose-6-phosphatase is an enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum in liver and kidney. It is not located in the mitochondrial membrane and plays no role in oxidative phosphorylation.

answers.text: A smooth, unfolded surface to minimise electron leakage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The inner membrane is extensively folded into cristae, which increase surface area for the ETC complexes and ATP synthase. Cells with high energy demands have densely packed cristae.

overallFeedback.feedback: The inner mitochondrial membrane must be impermeable to protons. This allows Complexes I, III, and IV to build an electrochemical gradient across it. ATP synthase then harnesses the controlled flow of protons back into the matrix to drive ATP production.
Correct. The impermeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane to protons is the foundation of chemiosmotic ATP synthesis — without it, the proton gradient could not be maintained.

interactions.label: Complex II of the electron transport chain pumps protons across the inner mitoch

params.question: Complex II of the electron transport chain pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, just like Complexes I, III, and IV.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Complex II is unique — it does NOT pump protons. The energy released by its electron transfer (succinate → FAD → Fe-S → CoQ) is insufficient to drive proton translocation across the membrane. Because Complex II bypasses the proton-pumping step of Complex I, electrons from FADH₂ generate fewer ATP molecules (~1.5 vs ~2.5 per NADH).
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is the only ETC complex that does NOT pump protons. The free energy released during the succinate → fumarate reaction and subsequent electron transfer to CoQ is too small to drive proton translocation. This is why electrons entering via FADH₂ at Complex II yield only ~1.5 ATP, compared to ~2.5 ATP for NADH entering at Complex I.

interactions.label: Cyanide, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen sulphide all inhibit cellular respiration

params.question: Cyanide, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen sulphide all inhibit cellular respiration by the same mechanism. What is it?

answers.text: They block electron donation from NADH at Complex I

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complex I inhibitors include rotenone, barbiturates, and MPTP — not cyanide, CO, or H₂S. These three poisons act much further downstream in the electron transport chain.

answers.text: They bind at the haem a₃–CuB centre of Complex IV, preventing oxygen reduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: All three poisons target the binuclear centre (haem a₃ paired with CuB) of Complex IV, where molecular oxygen normally binds and is reduced to water. When this site is blocked, the entire chain backs up — NADH cannot be re-oxidised, the TCA cycle stalls, and cells shift to anaerobic glycolysis.

answers.text: They act as uncouplers, dissipating the proton gradient as heat

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Uncouplers like 2,4-dinitrophenol carry protons across the membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. Cyanide, CO, and H₂S do the opposite — they halt electron flow entirely, which actually preserves (or even increases) the gradient transiently.

answers.text: They inhibit cytochrome c, preventing electron transfer between Complexes III and IV

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cytochrome c is a mobile electron carrier, not the target. These poisons act at Complex IV's active site where oxygen is reduced, not at the electron-receiving step from cytochrome c.

overallFeedback.feedback: Cyanide, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen sulphide all bind at Complex IV's haem a₃–CuB binuclear centre, the site where molecular oxygen is normally reduced to water. This blocks the final step of electron transport, shutting down the entire chain.

Correct. The haem a₃–CuB binuclear centre is the oxygen-binding site of Complex IV. All three poisons block oxygen access, halting the entire electron transport chain. In India, common sources include improperly processed cassava (cyanide), charcoal heaters in closed rooms (CO), and sewer work (H₂S).

interactions.label: According to Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, how is energy from the electron

params.question: According to Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis, how is energy from the electron transport chain coupled to ATP synthesis?

answers.text: Through a high-energy phosphorylated chemical intermediate linking the ETC to ATP synthase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This was the classical hypothesis that Mitchell disproved. The prevailing theory before 1961 assumed a chemical intermediate existed, similar to substrate-level phosphorylation. Mitchell showed the coupling is entirely indirect.

answers.text: By direct transfer of electrons from Complex IV to the catalytic site of ATP synthase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Electrons do not flow from the ETC to ATP synthase. The ETC and ATP synthase are coupled indirectly — the chain pumps protons, and ATP synthase is driven by their return flow, not by electrons.

answers.text: Through an electrochemical proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mitchell's key insight: Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons into the intermembrane space, creating both a chemical gradient (pH difference) and an electrical gradient (charge difference). This proton-motive force (~200 mV) drives protons back through ATP synthase, powering ATP production. No chemical intermediate is needed.

answers.text: By substrate-level phosphorylation within the mitochondrial matrix

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Substrate-level phosphorylation (e.g., in glycolysis) involves direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate to ADP. Oxidative phosphorylation is fundamentally different — it uses the energy stored in a proton gradient, which is Mitchell's central insight.

overallFeedback.feedback: Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis states that electron transport and ATP synthesis are coupled indirectly through an electrochemical proton gradient. There is no chemical intermediate. The proton-motive force has two components: a pH gradient and an electrical potential, totalling ~200 mV.

Correct. The chemiosmotic hypothesis — that energy coupling is entirely indirect via a proton gradient — is considered one of the most elegant ideas in biology. Mitchell received the Nobel Prize for this in 1978.

params.question: A patient presents with dangerously elevated body temperature after ingesting 2,4-dinitrophenol as a weight-loss agent. Which mechanism explains this hyperthermia?

answers.text: Inhibition of Complex IV, blocking all electron flow and causing cellular energy failure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complex IV inhibitors (e.g., cyanide) halt the electron transport chain entirely. DNP does the opposite — it allows the chain to run at maximum speed. The distinction is critical: inhibitors stop respiration; uncouplers accelerate it but waste the energy as heat.

answers.text: Dissipation of the proton gradient across the inner membrane, releasing energy as heat instead of ATP

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: DNP is a lipid-soluble weak acid that shuttles protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. The proton gradient collapses, so the ETC runs unchecked (maximum O₂ consumption) but produces no ATP. All the energy is released as heat. The physiological equivalent — thermogenin (UCP-1) in brown adipose tissue — performs the same function safely for non-shivering thermogenesis in newborns.

answers.text: Overstimulation of ATP synthase, producing excessive ATP that drives exothermic reactions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Uncouplers actually reduce ATP synthesis by dissipating the proton gradient that ATP synthase needs. The heat comes from the uncontrolled electron transport itself, not from excess ATP production.

answers.text: Blockade of the proton channel in ATP synthase, causing the gradient to build dangerously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes oligomycin's mechanism, not an uncoupler's. Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase, causing the gradient to build up. This actually slows electron transport (respiratory control). DNP works in the opposite direction — it dissipates the gradient.

overallFeedback.feedback: 2,4-Dinitrophenol is an uncoupler — a lipid-soluble weak acid that carries protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. The proton gradient collapses, the ETC accelerates without restraint, and all energy is dissipated as heat. This is why it causes fatal hyperthermia.

Correct. Uncouplers like DNP dissipate the proton gradient, so the ETC runs at full speed but produces no ATP — all energy escapes as heat. DNP was banned as a weight-loss drug in the 1930s after causing fatal hyperthermia. The body uses the same principle safely via UCP-1 in brown fat.
